Sparse rewards and curiosity

When the only reward is at the far end of a maze, every value is zero until the agent stumbles on it, and ε-greedy stumbles slowly. A curious agent pays itself a small bonus for going somewhere new. The bonus fades with familiarity, so it keeps pushing towards the parts of the maze it knows least.

Count bonus

agent visits $N(s)$, darker = more G: the only reward

The four-room gridworld (Sutton, Precup & Singh, 1999). Each episode starts at S and lasts at most 100 steps. Reward $+1$ at G, 0 everywhere else. Both agents run Q-learning with $\alpha = 0.1$, $\gamma = 0.95$, $\varepsilon = 0.1$. The right one adds $\beta/\sqrt{N(s')}$ to every reward, with visit counts kept across episodes.

How often is the goal found?

Fraction of 40 independent runs that have reached G at least once, by episode.

The maths

With reward only at G and all values starting at 0, Q-learning's targets $R + \gamma \max_a Q(S', a)$ are all 0 until the first arrival. Before that, ε-greedy with random tie-breaking is a random walk. A random walk spreads out like $\sqrt{t}$, so crossing a maze takes a number of steps that grows with the square of its size, and doorways make it worse.

A count-based bonus adds an intrinsic reward for reaching $s'$:

$$\tilde R_{t+1} = R_{t+1} + \frac{\beta}{\sqrt{N(S_{t+1})}}$$

$N(s)$ counts visits to $s$ so far, including this one. A first visit pays $\beta$, the hundredth pays $\beta/10$. Well-trodden states stop paying, so their values sink below those of places seldom seen. Bellemare et al. (2016) extended this to images by estimating "pseudo-counts" from a density model, which made progress on Montezuma's Revenge, an Atari game where ε-greedy DQN scores almost nothing.

One detail matters. An action never tried has $Q = 0$, but a tried one has collected bonuses and has $Q > 0$. A greedy agent would then prefer what it already knows. So the bonus agent starts every value at the most a stream of bonuses could be worth:

$$Q_0 = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k \beta = \frac{\beta}{1 - \gamma}$$

This is Lesson 8's optimism, sized to the bonus. Untried actions look as good as anything can, until tried.

Curiosity (Pathak et al., 2017) replaces counts with surprise. A forward model predicts the features of the next state, $\hat\phi(s_{t+1})$, and the bonus is its error:

$$r^i_t = \frac{\eta}{2} \big\lVert \hat\phi(s_{t+1}) - \phi(s_{t+1}) \big\rVert^2$$

Places the model cannot yet predict pay well. Once learned, they stop paying, just as a count does. Pure noise (a TV showing static) stays unpredictable forever, so a naive curious agent can get stuck watching it.
